title: Always-on, highly efficient microwave photon detector based on a superconducting artificial molecule
authors: Vyom Kulkarni, Mohammed Ali Aamir, Simon Sundelin, Simone Gasparinetti
abstract: Efficient detection of single microwave photons is a key capability for emerging quantum technologies. Yet, it remains far less developed than its optical domain counterpart. Realizing detectors that simultaneously achieve high efficiency, low dark counts, and continuous operation has proved challenging. Existing detectors operate cyclically, forcing a trade-off between efficiency and duty cycle. Here, we demonstrate a continuously operated microwave single-photon detector based on a superconducting artificial molecule. In our scheme, an incoming photon is captured by a bright state of the molecule and then transferred to a long-lived dark state via a driven-dissipative process. Photon ``clicks'' are revealed as quantum jumps in the continuously monitored dark state. We observe a cyclic detection efficiency of $0.73$, and a continuous detection efficiency of $0.47$ over a $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$ instantaneous bandwidth, with a $1\,μ\mathrm{s}$ temporal resolution and a $15\,μ\mathrm{s}$ dead time. By overcoming the trade-off between efficiency and duty cycle, this approach establishes continuous microwave photon detection for quantum sensing, quantum thermodynamics, and fundamental physics.
summary: The paper presents an experimental realization of a continuously operating microwave single-photon detector using a superconducting artificial molecule. By engineering the system dynamics to transfer absorbed photons into a continuously monitored state, they overcome the efficiency vs. duty cycle trade-off inherent in prior detectors. This breakthrough enables continuous quantum measurement crucial for quantum sensing and thermodynamics.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing a microwave single-photon detector that achieves high efficiency, low dark counts, and continuous operation simultaneously, overcoming limitations of existing cyclic detectors.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a continuously operated detector with a measured efficiency of 0.47, successfully establishing a method for continuous microwave photon detection in quantum technologies.
method: The experiment involves characterizing the system's response using both pulsed (cyclic) and continuous readout protocols, analyzing quantum jumps and signal-to-noise ratios.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a superconducting artificial molecule built from two coupled transmon qubits. The dynamics are modeled as a four-level system involving symmetric ($	ext{S}$) and anti-symmetric ($	ext{A}$) modes, driven by photon absorption into the $	ext{S}$ mode and monitored via continuous readout of the $	ext{A}$ mode.
key_observables: Continuous detection efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{cont}} = 0.47$), dark count rate ($1.3 	ext{ kHz}$), temporal resolution ($1\ \mu	ext{s}$), and dead time ($15\ \mu	ext{s}$).
important_parameters: Operating temperature of $8 	ext{ mK}$; coupling rate $\Gamma_s/2\pi = 7.26 	ext{ MHz}$.
main_assumptions: The continuous efficiency is modeled as a product of the intrinsic absorption efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{abs}}$) and the readout fidelity factor ($F_{	ext{cont}}$), which are both dependent on measurement strength.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the operating principle, spectroscopy of the symmetric mode, dispersive readout of the anti-symmetric mode, and the photon transfer mechanism from $	ext{S}$ to $	ext{A}$.
paper_structure: The work progresses by first characterizing the system modes (spectroscopy), then demonstrating pulsed detection efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{cyc}}$), and finally establishing continuous operation by modeling the trade-off between absorption and readout fidelity.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it uses superconducting circuits—a platform for engineered quantum matter—to solve a fundamental problem in quantum optics: efficient, continuous single-photon detection.
